92.title: Take and read
92.hook: in a Milan garden Augustine hears a child's voice say take and read, and his long restlessness ends (Confessions 8)
92.howItsDone: Augustine's conversion is remembered by Christians across the churches, and his line about the restless heart is often quoted. Some Christians read a short passage of scripture each day, and let one verse speak to them as he did.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Monica's tears, and a bishop's promise. Your line was tears are not wasted.

Tomorrow is a very comfortable word. The habit you'll quit tomorrow. And then tomorrow. Milan. Augustine is a successful teacher of speaking, career on the rise, and he is falling apart. He's become convinced the faith his mother prayed for is true, but he can't make himself step into it. He writes that he was bound, not by iron chains, but by his own will. One day, with his friend Alypius, in the garden of the house where they're staying, it all comes to a head. He goes off alone under a fig tree, throws himself down, and weeps. How long? Tomorrow, and tomorrow? Why not now?
screen: `TOMORROW, AND TOMORROW.` → `A GARDEN IN MILAN.` → `UNDER A FIG TREE, WEEPING.`

segments.voice: Then, Augustine says, he heard a voice from a house next door, like a child's, chanting over and over: take up and read, take up and read. In Latin, tolle lege. He stops crying and tries to think of any children's game that uses those words. He can't, so he takes it as a command. He remembers Antony, the desert monk, who once walked into church, heard a Gospel line read aloud, and took it as spoken to him. So Augustine hurries back to where Alypius is sitting, where he'd left a book of Paul's letters, snatches it up, and reads the first thing his eyes fall on. Romans thirteen, in the King James Bible: "not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying. But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." He says he didn't want or need to read further. It was as if a light of peace flooded his heart, and the dark of doubt ran away. Alypius reads the next line, about welcoming the one who is weak in faith, and takes it for himself. The two go straight inside to tell Monica, who, he says, leapt for joy. Years later, Augustine opened his Confessions with a line spoken to God: you made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. That garden was where his restlessness met its rest. One caution some Christian teachers add: this isn't a recipe for opening the Bible like a fortune cookie. Augustine's moment came after years of searching, reading, arguing and being prayed for.

segments.voice: Open any book nearby at random, a Bible if you have one, a novel, a poetry book, a cookbook, and read one sentence slowly. Don't hunt for a better one. Read it again. Ask what it might say to you today; if nothing, that's fine, you've still stopped. If you pray, you can ask God to speak through what you read.
Tolle lege. Latin for take up and read, the words a child's voice seemed to chant in a Milan garden.

93.title: Francis and the birds
93.hook: a rich man's son gives it all away and preaches to the birds, who stay to listen (Little Flowers 16)
93.howItsDone: Saint Francis's feast day is October 4, and Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches often hold a blessing of the animals on or near it. The hymn 'All Creatures of Our God and King' is based on his Canticle of the Creatures.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tolle lege: a child's voice in a Milan garden, and one verse. Your line was our heart is restless.

Assisi, a hill town in Italy. In front of the bishop and a crowd, a rich cloth merchant is furious with his son, Francis, who has been giving away the family's money and goods to rebuild a ruined chapel and feed the poor. The father wants it all back. So Francis takes off his clothes, every piece, and hands them to his father. From now on, he says, I can say freely, our Father who art in heaven. The bishop wraps him in his own cloak, and the party boy of Assisi walks out of town with nothing. Years later, on a road in the Umbrian countryside, he stops: the trees are full of birds.
screen: `A FATHER, A SON, A BISHOP.` → `HE HANDS BACK HIS CLOTHES.` → `TREES FULL OF BIRDS.`

segments.voice: One of his early biographers, Thomas of Celano, tells this, and the later Little Flowers of Saint Francis retells it with more color. Francis tells his companions, wait here, I'm going to preach to my little sisters, the birds. In the field he tells them they owe God a lot of praise: for their feathers, for the freedom to fly anywhere, for rivers and springs to drink from, for food they never had to plant or harvest, echoing Jesus's words about the birds of the air. And the story says the birds stay. They open their beaks, stretch out their necks, bow their heads, and don't fly away until he blesses them. Then they rise and scatter in four directions, like a cross. The Little Flowers mix memory with loving legend, and nobody knows exactly what happened there. But the heart of it matches his early lives: to him the whole world was family. Near the end of his life, sick and nearly blind, he wrote a song of praise in his home's Umbrian dialect, not church Latin: the Canticle of the Creatures. It praises God for brother sun, and sister moon and the stars, brother wind, sister water, brother fire, and our sister, mother earth. At the very end, he even welcomes sister death. Some churches bless animals on his feast day. A pope in our own time took his name, and titled a letter about caring for the earth with the canticle's refrain, praised be you.

94.title: Teresa of Ávila
94.hook: a nun who laughed, founded convents on the road, and said prayer is friendship
94.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Teresa of Ávila's feast on October 15, and her books, especially The Interior Castle and The Way of Perfection, are read by Christians of many churches as guides to prayer. Discalced Carmelite nuns still live by her reform.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Little Flowers: Francis and the birds, and a song for all creation. Your line was brother sun, sister moon.

Spain, the 1570s. A covered wagon lurches along a muddy road in the rain, pulled by mules, packed with a few nuns, their bags, and a woman nearing sixty who is running the whole operation. Her name is Teresa, from the walled city of Ávila. She's buying houses, dealing with lawyers and bishops, borrowing money, finding cooks, and opening one small convent after another across the country. She's funny; her letters are full of gossip, jokes and health complaints. And in the middle of all this driving and deal-making, she's famous for prayer. Not solemn, faraway prayer. The kind you'd have with a friend over a kitchen table.
screen: `A WAGON IN THE RAIN.` → `RUNNING THE WHOLE OPERATION.` → `FAMOUS FOR PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Teresa was born in 1515 and entered a Carmelite convent at about twenty. For almost twenty years, she says, prayer was a struggle. She was often ill, distracted, and couldn't wait for the hour of prayer to end. At around forty, something opened, and she spent the rest of her life trying to explain it. Her best-known description is in her life story, written because her confessors asked. Prayer, she says, is nothing else than close sharing between friends: taking time, often, to be alone with the one we know loves us. Friendship. Not performance, not a list of requests. Time with a friend who happens to be God. Later she wrote The Interior Castle, picturing the soul as a castle of one clear crystal, with many rooms, and God living in the very center. Prayer is the door in. She reformed her order, founding houses where the nuns lived simply, and worked with a young friar who became Saint John of the Cross. She died in 1582. In 1970, the Catholic Church named her a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for everyone; she and Catherine of Siena were the first women given that title. And she laughed. People still tell a story, not found in her writings, of her tipping out of a cart into the mud and complaining to God, and hearing, this is how I treat my friends, and answering, then it's no wonder you have so few. Whether or not it happened, it sounds like someone who talked to God as a friend.

segments.voice: If you pray, try Teresa's way: no formal words, just tell God about today as you'd tell a close friend, what annoyed you, what made you laugh, what worries you, then be quiet a moment to let your friend answer. If not, picture someone who knows you completely and likes you anyway, and tell them.

95.title: Joan of Arc
95.hook: a teenage peasant hears voices, leads an army, is burned at nineteen, and is declared innocent too late
95.tomorrow: Camp 2 close: the story you're in
95.howItsDone: Joan of Arc is honored as a saint by the Catholic Church, with a feast day on May 30, and as a patron saint of France. Christians of many churches admire her courage and her answers at her trial.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa of Ávila and her Interior Castle. Your line was prayer is friendship.

Think of yourself at thirteen: your worries, what you thought you could do. Now, a village called Domrémy, in eastern France, around the year 1425. France has been at war with England for generations, and much of the north is occupied. A peasant girl named Jeanne, Joan, can't read or write. She spins wool and helps in the fields. She says that in her father's garden she began to hear voices, which she came to know as Saint Michael, Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret. They tell her to be good and go to church. Over the next few years, they tell her something impossible: go to the king's heir, and help drive the English out.
screen: `YOU, AT THIRTEEN.` → `A GIRL IN DOMRÉMY.` → `VOICES IN THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: At seventeen, Joan talks her way past soldiers and nobles to Charles, the uncrowned heir, and somehow convinces him. She's given armor and a banner, and in the spring of 1429 she rides with the army to the besieged city of Orléans. Within days the siege is broken. That summer she stands beside Charles as he's crowned king at Reims. A year later she's captured, sold to the English, and put on trial at Rouen by a church court of clergy loyal to the English. The trial record survives, and it's astonishing. For weeks, learned men question an unlettered nineteen-year-old, trying to trap her. The most famous trap: do you know you are in God's grace? Say yes, and she's claiming a certainty no one can have. Say no, and she's confessing guilt. She answers, in effect: if I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God keep me so. The court falls silent. They condemn her anyway. On the thirtieth of May, 1431, she's burned in the marketplace at Rouen, asking for a cross to be held before her eyes, and calling on the name of Jesus. Twenty-five years later a new church trial declared the verdict null: she'd been innocent. Too late. In 1920 the Catholic Church named her a saint. What were her voices? People explain them many ways; the sources can't settle it. She's often quoted as saying, I am not afraid; I was born to do this. Historians can't find that line in the records. But her answers at the trial show the same thing. She wasn't afraid.
screen: `ORLÉANS, THEN REIMS.` · `NINETEEN, AGAINST LEARNED MEN.` · `IF I AM NOT, MAY GOD PUT ME THERE.` · `INNOCENT, TWENTY-FIVE YEARS LATE.` · then, large: `I AM NOT AFRAID.`

96.title: Camp 2 close: the story you're in
96.hook: parables, a birth, a road, a cross, an empty tomb, a church on the move
96.howItsDone: Christians retell these stories every year through the church calendar, from the annunciation and Christmas through Holy Week, Easter and Pentecost, and remember the saints on their feast days. Many churches read the Gospels and Acts in order across the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joan of Arc at Rouen. Your line was I am not afraid. Today, the last of the stories.

Seventy-five days of stories. A farmer sowing on every kind of ground. A woman sweeping the house for one coin. A servant who buried his talent because he was afraid. A young woman in Nazareth saying, let it be. A feeding trough. Shepherds on the night shift. Fishermen told to put out into the deep. A short man up a tree. A king on a donkey. A towel and a basin. A rooster. A cross. A garden, and a name said kindly. Then a road to Emmaus, a charcoal fire, wind and flame, a jailer, a shipwreck, a letter full of names. And saints: a mother's tears, a garden in Milan, birds, a wagon in the rain, a girl in armor.
screen: `SEED, COIN, TALENT.` → `A TROUGH, A CROSS, A GARDEN.` → `A FIRE, A FLAME, A SHIPWRECK.`

segments.voice: Mark's Gospel, the shortest, begins, in the King James Bible: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." The beginning. Gospel is the old English godspel, good news, translating the Greek euangelion. The Gospels tell it as a story, not a list of ideas: parables that turn things upside down, a birth in the wrong place, a road through Galilee, one last week in Jerusalem, a cross, and an empty tomb. And the book of Acts, where this camp has lived for weeks, doesn't end. Its last scene: Paul under house arrest in Rome two whole years, welcoming all who came, teaching, in the King James words, "with all confidence, no man forbidding him." Then Luke stops. Acts never tells Paul's trial or his death. Some readers take that open ending as deliberate: the story keeps going. Through Stephen and Philip and Lydia, then Monica and Augustine, Francis, Teresa, Joan, and names nobody wrote down. Christians say every life that takes it up becomes another page. That doesn't mean anyone here has to believe it. Some of you walk this path because it's your faith, some because it's someone else's you love, some just to understand. You've walked its length now, from the sower to the shipwreck. Next, this path moves from stories to practices: how Christians pray, sing, rest and live it, day to day. Camp three begins tomorrow. You're in the story now.

97.title: What prayer is
97.hook: less about getting words right, more like talking and listening to someone who's already there
97.howItsDone: Christians pray alone and together: many use set prayers such as the Lord's Prayer and the prayers of their church's liturgy, many pray in their own words, and some wait in silence. Many pray at set times, such as morning, evening and before meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, euangelion, the good news, closed seventy-five days of stories. Your line was you're in the story now. Today, camp three: the practices.

A hospital waiting room. A plane in bad turbulence. The night before the results come back. Please. Just, please. Sometimes it comes out before anyone decides to say it, even from people who'd never call themselves religious. And some who've gone to church their whole lives say prayer is the part they feel worst at: wrong words, wrong posture, wandering mind, nothing happening. For the next few weeks, this path turns from stories to practices, the things Christians actually do, day to day, starting with the most basic. What is prayer, actually? Christians would say: less about getting the words right than you'd think.
screen: `PLEASE. JUST, PLEASE.` → `AM I DOING IT WRONG?` → `FROM STORIES TO PRACTICES.`

segments.voice: English pray comes, through old French, from the Latin precari: to ask, to beg. Asking is part of it. But the Christian tradition keeps insisting prayer is bigger than a request line. It's talking and listening, to someone who, Christians say, is already there before you start. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says don't pray to be seen. "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret." A closet: a small, private room. Don't pile up words, either, thinking more words get you heard, "for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him." So why pray at all, if God already knows? Christians have given many answers, but a common one: prayer isn't about informing God. It's about being with him. That's the talking half. The listening half is just as old. In the Hebrew Bible, a boy named Samuel keeps hearing his name called in the night, and an old priest teaches him what to say: "Speak; for thy servant heareth." The prophet Elijah looks for God in a great wind, an earthquake and a fire, and finds him instead in a still small voice. Christians pray in many ways. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran Christians often use set prayers, words handed down for centuries. Many evangelical and Pentecostal Christians pray freely, in their own words. Quakers often wait together in silence. The next days will try several. Under all of them is one simple shape. Talk, then listen.

segments.voice: If you pray, say one honest sentence to God; if you don't, say it into the quiet: what you're grateful for, afraid of, or need. Then stop and listen for a minute. You may hear only your breath and the room; that's fine, listening is the practice, not hearing.
Prayer. From the Latin for asking, and for Christians something wider: talking and listening to God. Camp three's first word.

98.title: A simple pattern
98.hook: many Protestant churches teach adoration, confession, thanksgiving, supplication as a shape for prayer
98.howItsDone: Many Protestant, especially evangelical, churches teach ACTS (adoration, confession, thanksgiving, supplication) as a pattern for personal and group prayer. Churches with set liturgies follow a similar movement of praise, confession, thanks and intercession in their services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prayer: from the Latin for asking, and wider than asking. Your line was talk, then listen. Fourteen weeks on the path.

Blank-page panic. You sit down to write a birthday card, a toast, a hard email, and nothing comes. Then someone says: just do three things. Say what you love about them, tell one story, raise your glass. Suddenly it's easy. A shape helps. Prayer goes the same way. Eyes close, and the mind goes blank, or straight to a shopping list: help me, fix that. So many Protestant churches, especially evangelical ones, teach a four-letter shape to hang a prayer on. It spells a book of the Bible you've just spent weeks in. A, C, T, S.
screen: `BLANK-PAGE PANIC.` → `JUST DO THREE THINGS.` → `A, C, T, S.`

segments.voice: A is for adoration. Before asking anything, you start with who God is, the way the Psalms do: "O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker." Not thanks yet; just wonder at who he is. C is for confession: being honest about where you've gone wrong. The first letter of John puts it simply: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins." Catholics and Orthodox also have confession as a sacrament with a priest; many Protestants confess directly to God, alone or together in a service. T is for thanksgiving: naming what you're grateful for, specifically. S is for supplication, an old word for asking, humbly, for yourself and for others. Paul packs almost the whole shape into one line to the church in Philippi: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God." Be careful for nothing means don't be anxious about anything. Notice the order: asking comes last. By then you've remembered who you're talking to, been honest, and said thank you, and the asking often comes out different. Nobody knows exactly who first put these four letters together; it's a modern teaching tool, not a verse. But the shape is old. The Lord's Prayer says hallowed be thy name before it gets to daily bread, and many written liturgies follow a similar path. ACTS just carries it in your pocket.
screen: `A: ADORATION.` · `C: CONFESSION.` · `T: THANKSGIVING.` · `S: SUPPLICATION.` · then, large: `A SHAPE HELPS.`

segments.voice: If you pray, go through the four letters slowly, one sentence each: one thing about God that fills you with wonder, one honest thing you got wrong, one specific thing from today, one thing you or someone else needs. Leave a little silence between each. If you don't pray, try the shape anyway: something that fills you with wonder, something you'd do differently, something you're grateful for, something you hope for.
ACTS. Adoration, confession, thanksgiving, supplication. This week: take and read, Francis, Teresa, Joan, the story you're in, prayer, and a shape.
